title: How to Set Up Team Roles and Artwork Approvals in an Apliiq Catalog
excerpt: Shared logins and informal approvals are how custom apparel catalogs get expensive. This setup gives each person a defined role, puts a review gate between upload and listing, and keeps file versions readable long after launch.
body: One shared login is how a print-on-demand catalog gets expensive. Someone uploads artwork to the wrong product, someone else orders a sample on the live card, a third person answers a customer with a promise production cannot keep, and nobody can tell who did what. The fix is not more trust or more meetings. It is a small role model, a review step before anything reaches a listing, and a naming convention that survives staff turnover.

Define four roles and keep them separate even when two people share the work. The catalog owner decides what gets listed and at what price. The artwork reviewer checks files against print rules and approves or rejects. The sample buyer places and evaluates test orders. Support reads production status and answers customers but does not change artwork. Write the four roles on one page with the actions each may take, and grant access at that level rather than sharing an admin password with a contractor.

Put the approval between upload and publish. A design should move through three states: uploaded, reviewed, approved for listing. Only the reviewer moves a file from reviewed to approved, and only approved files are allowed onto a product page. This single gate prevents the most common expensive mistake in custom apparel, which is a beautiful mockup printed at the wrong size because nobody compared the actual print dimensions against the garment template.

Name files so the version is visible without opening them. A workable pattern is collection, design name, garment, placement, version and date. When a buyer asks for a change two weeks after launch, the reviewer finds the approved file instead of guessing which of four similarly named uploads went live. Keep rejected files in a separate folder with the rejection reason in the file name, because the reason is the useful part of a rejection six months later.

Give the sample buyer a written scorecard: print sharpness, color match against the approved file, placement against the template, stitching at stress points, and how the garment behaves after one wash. A sample that passes the first three and fails on wash performance is a return waiting to happen, and learning that on one unit is far cheaper than learning it on forty orders. Record the verdict next to the version number so the decision travels with the file.

Document the handover. A new team member should be able to place a sample, read the approval queue and answer a status question within an hour of getting access, using only a two page guide and the folder structure. Review the role list each quarter and remove access for anyone who has left the catalog, since dormant admin accounts on a supplier portal are an avoidable risk. The DTCwise Print-on-Demand category at /category/pod keeps the current platform shortlist, and /tool/apliiq covers the production side of custom apparel.
